question: A newborn is identified with bilateral severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss on universal newborn hearing screening. The parents have normal hearing and there is no family history of deafness. Which statement about the aetiology is most accurate?

answers.text: The hearing loss is most likely due to perinatal hypoxia since both parents have normal hearing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While perinatal hypoxia can cause hearing loss, approximately 50% of congenital SNHL is genetic. Autosomal recessive inheritance (non-syndromic) is the most common genetic pattern, which means both parents can be asymptomatic carriers with normal hearing and still produce an affected child.

answers.text: Approximately 50% of congenital SNHL is genetic, and the most common single-gene cause in non-syndromic deafness is a mutation in the GJB2 gene (Connexin 26)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. About 50% of congenital SNHL is genetic. Of genetic causes, 70% are non-syndromic, and of these, ~50% are due to GJB2 (Connexin 26) mutations — the single most common genetic cause of congenital deafness worldwide. Autosomal recessive inheritance explains normal hearing in carrier parents.

answers.text: Congenital rubella is now the most common cause of congenital deafness in India

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. With rubella immunisation programmes, congenital rubella syndrome has become less common. Genetic causes (especially GJB2/Connexin 26) account for approximately 50% of congenital SNHL overall. Environmental/acquired causes include CMV, hyperbilirubinaemia, and aminoglycosides — but rubella is no longer the dominant cause.

answers.text: Normal hearing in both parents excludes a genetic cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The most common pattern of genetic deafness (DFNB1/GJB2) is autosomal recessive. Both parents are asymptomatic carriers with normal hearing, but each has a 25% chance with every pregnancy of producing an affected child. Normal parental hearing never excludes autosomal recessive deafness.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key fact: 50% of congenital SNHL is genetic. Of genetic cases, GJB2 (Connexin 26) is the most common single-gene cause, transmitted in an autosomal recessive pattern. Normal hearing in both parents does NOT exclude genetic deafness — they are carriers.

Correct. About 50% of congenital SNHL is genetic; GJB2 (Connexin 26) is the single most common gene. Autosomal recessive inheritance explains normal-hearing carrier parents. Genetic testing (GJB2 mutation analysis) is part of the workup for all congenital SNHL.
